Summary and guiding principles
- Client: 36‑yr male recreational lifter, cleared for low‑impact strength work after right medial meniscus tear (6 months post‑op). No jumping and no deep knee flexion under load (avoid loaded knee flexion beyond ~90°; avoid deep squats, heavy lunges with deep knee angles, plyometrics).
- Goal: rebuild strength, restore balanced lower‑limb control and resilience for skiing next season while protecting knee.
- Program structure: 12 weeks divided into 3 phases (Accumulation / Hypertrophy 4 weeks; Intensification / Strength 4 weeks; Peak / Ski‑specific strength and robustness 4 weeks). 4 training days per week (upper/lower split with an emphasis on unilateral work and posterior chain, plus mobility/conditioning). Progressive overload built by increasing load or intensity each week, with deload built in week 4 and week 8 options if needed.
- Key exercise selection rules: avoid deep knee flexion under heavy load; prefer box squat (box at ~90° or higher), belt squats, split squats with reduced range, step‑ups to mid‑height, Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts, Nordic or eccentric hamstring work where tolerated, cable/band work for dynamic control, and single‑leg balance/strength. Use machines (leg press with limited ROM) to control depth. Emphasize glute and hamstring strength, knee dynamic stability, hip external rotation, and core. Controlled tempo and good technique are essential.
- Progression and RPE: aim for 2.5–5% load increase or +1–2 reps when plan targets achieved. Work sets at RPE 7–9 depending on phase. If any knee pain >3/10, regress ROM/load.
- Warm‑up: 8–12 min general cardio low impact (bike/row), dynamic mobility, and movement prep focusing on hip hinge, glute activation, and single‑leg control. Include 2–3 warm‑up sets before main lifts.
- Recovery: sleep 7–9 h, adequate protein (1.6–2.0 g/kg/day), caloric intake adjusted to maintain or slight surplus if wanting to add muscle — for strength focus maintenance or modest +200 kcal/day. Hydration and anti‑inflammatory measures as needed. Foam rolling, targeted soft tissue work, and nightly mobility routine for knee and hips. Avoid prolonged deep knee flexion (kneeling chairs) early in day if symptomatic.
- Precautions: no jump training, no heavy loaded deep squats >90°, avoid loaded knee flexion with valgus collapse. Use knee sleeves for comfort if desired. Communicate with surgeon/physio if any unusual swelling, catching, or instability.

Weekly schedule (4 days)
- Day A: Lower primary — Posterior chain & Quad controlled patterns (heavy)
- Day B: Upper push/pull (horizontal emphasis)
- Day C: Lower secondary — Unilateral + Knee control + Hip stability (moderate)
- Day D: Upper push/pull (vertical emphasis) + core/anti‑rotation

Phases overview
Phase 1: Weeks 1–4 — Accumulation (hypertrophy & movement quality)
- Goal: build tissue capacity, correct imbalances, teach safe movement patterns, higher volume, moderate intensity.
- Typical loads: 65–75% 1RM or RPE 6–8; sets 3–4, reps 8–12 for most compound lifts.

Phase 2: Weeks 5–8 — Intensification (strength)
- Goal: increase neural strength, lower rep ranges, increase load while keeping ROM safe.
- Typical loads: 75–90% 1RM or RPE 7–9; sets 3–5, reps 3–6 for main lifts; maintain accessory volume.

Phase 3: Weeks 9–12 — Peak / Ski specific strength & robustness
- Goal: convert strength into ski‑relevant strength and control: tempo, isometrics, unilateral loaded control, higher force production without impact.
- Typical loads: heavy singles to 3s on main lifts but controlled depth, plus eccentrics and slow isometrics. Include skiing mimic conditioning (low‑impact lateral step machines, skierg).

Program details — week‑by‑week (all weeks use the same 4‑day order)

Phase 1 — Weeks 1–4 (Accumulation)
Notes: rest 90–120s for heavy lower compound sets, 60–90s for accessories.

Week 1
Day A — Lower (Strength focus, posterior chain priority)
- Warm up: 8–10 min bike + dynamic hip mobility + 2 warm‑up sets of main lift
- Main 1: Box Back Squat (box set to ~90° knee angle; focus on tempo 2s down, pause 1s, 1s up) — 4 × 8 @ moderate load (RPE 7)
- Main 2: Romanian Deadlift (RDL) — 4 × 8 (focus hip hinge)
- Accessory 1: Single‑leg Romanian Deadlift (DB) — 3 × 8/leg
- Accessory 2: Glute Bridge / Hip Thrust (barbell, feet placement to limit knee flexion) — 3 × 10
- Accessory 3: Seated/Standing Calf Raises — 3 × 12
- Core: Pallof press 3 × 10/side

Day B — Upper (Horizontal)
- Bench Press 4 × 8
- Bent Over Row or Chest‑supported Row 4 × 8
- Incline DB Press 3 × 10
- Lat Pulldown 3 × 10
- Face Pulls 3 × 15
- Biceps 2 × 10; Triceps 2 × 10

Day C — Lower (Unilateral + Stability)
- Warm up: same pattern, add single‑leg balance drills
- Main 1: Split Squat (rear foot elevated or Bulgarian?) — use reduced range to keep front knee ≤90°; 3 × 8/leg
- Main 2: Step‑ups to mid height (box about knee height or lower) — 3 × 8/leg
- Accessory: Cable Pull‑throughs or Kettlebell Swings (light, hinge emphasis, no ballistic jumping) — 3 × 12
- Accessory: Nordic hamstring negatives (assisted) 3 × 6 (match tolerance)
- Lateral band walk 3 × 20 steps
- Core: Dead bug 3 × 10/side

Day D — Upper (Vertical / Conditioning)
- Standing Overhead Press (strict) 4 × 8
- Pull‑ups or Assisted Pull‑ups 4 × 6–8
- Seated DB Shoulder Press 3 × 10
- Single‑arm Cable Row 3 × 10/arm
- Farmer Carrys (moderate) 3 × 40–60m
- Core: Plank 3 × 45–60s

Week 2
- Increase main compound load ~2–5% or +1 rep where possible.
- Keep sets/reps same as Week 1.
- Add 1 additional set to one accessory per session if recovered.

Week 3
- Slightly increase intensity again aiming RPE 7–8 on main lifts.
- Replace RDL one session with barbell good mornings (light) if comfortable for hamstrings/glutes.
- Continue Nordic eccentrics; progress depth slowly.

Week 4 (deload / consolidation)
- Reduce volume ~30% (drop sets or reps), keep loads moderate; focus on technique, mobility, and any physiotherapy exercises for knee. Example: main lifts 3 × 6 at lighter weight; maintain accessory light.

Phase 2 — Weeks 5–8 (Intensification)
Notes: shift to heavier loads, lower reps on main lifts. Still avoid deep knee flexion; use box/belt squat to protect knee.

Week 5
Day A — Lower (heavy)
- Box Back Squat 5 × 5 (work up to RPE 7–8)
- Barbell Hip Thrust 4 × 6–8 (heavy)
- Romanian Deadlift 3 × 6
- Bulgarian Split Squat (shallow range) 3 × 6/leg
- Standing Calf Raise 4 × 10
- Core: Farmers hold 3 × 60s

Day B — Upper (heavy)
- Bench Press 5 × 5
- Weighted Pull‑up 4 × 5–6
- Incline Bench 3 × 6–8
- Chest‑supported Row 3 × 6–8
- Rear delt fly 3 × 12

Day C — Lower (unilateral / control)
- Single‑leg Press (leg press with limited ROM, 0–90°) 4 × 6–8/leg (ensure knee not exceeding flexion limit)
- Reverse Lunges to mid ROM (or stepping back) 3 × 6/leg
- Nordic hamstring eccentrics 4 × 6 (increase eccentric control)
- Cable lateral shuffles or horizontal skier (low impact) 3 × 30s
- Glute medius work bands 3 × 15/side
- Core: Anti‑rotation Pallof 4 × 8/side

Day D — Upper (volume + power without jumping)
- Push Press (light to moderate, emphasis on hip drive, not heavy jerk) 4 × 4–6
- Dumbbell Rows 4 × 6–8
- Dips or weighted dips 3 × 6–8
- Face pulls 3 × 15
- Farmer carry or suitcase carry heavy 4 × 40m
- Core: Hanging leg raise or knees to chest 3 × 10

Week 6
- Increase loads 2.5–5% on main lifts if week 5 felt manageable.
- Option: replace Box Squat with Belt Squat for one session if knee fatigues.

Week 7
- Main lifts move to heavier singles/doubles on last set — e.g., work sets 5 × 3 on squats or 4 × 4 with last set near RPE 8–9.
- Maintain unilateral control work and eccentrics.

Week 8 (deload)
- Reduce volume ~30–40%, keep intensity moderate. Focus mobility, technique, and ski‑specific conditioning drills (see phase 3 prep). Example: 3 × 3–5 at lighter weights, accessory 2 × 10.

Phase 3 — Weeks 9–12 (Peak / Ski‑specific strength & robustness)
Notes: blend heavy strength with ski‑specific unilateral control, isometrics, and low‑impact dynamic conditioning (skierg, lateral step machine, slideboard without jumping). Aim to produce force, control valgus, and manage eccentric demands encountered in skiing.

Week 9
Day A — Lower (peak strength)
- Belt Squat or Box Back Squat (higher load, tight ROM) — 5 × 3 (RPE 8–9)
- Barbell Hip Thrust 4 × 4–6 (heavy)
- Reverse Nordics or Controlled Eccentric Step downs (standing on box, lower slowly) 3 × 6–8/leg
- Staggered Stance Romanian Deadlift (focus posterior chain) 3 × 6/leg
- Calf raise heavy 4 × 8
- Core: Heavy suitcase carry 3 × 40m

Day B — Upper (strength)
- Bench Press 5 × 3 (heavy)
- Weighted Pull‑up 4 × 4
- Incline DB heavy 3 × 6
- Single‑arm row heavy 3 × 6
- Face pulls 3 × 12

Day C — Lower (ski specific + unilateral control)
- Lateral step‑downs or lateral box step‑overs (controlled) 4 × 6/side
- Single‑leg press with controlled eccentric (0–90°) 4 × 6/leg
- Isometric hold: 1‑leg squat to 90° box hold 3 × 15–20s/leg (if pain‑free)
- Eccentric‑accentuated RDL (3s down) 3 × 8
- Cable woodchoppers / rotational core 3 × 10/side

Day D — Upper + Conditioning
- Push press or strict press 4 × 4–6
- Bent over row 4 × 6
- Dips 3 × 6–8
- Skierg intervals: 6 × 30s on / 90s off (low impact conditioning) OR lateral stepper 6 × 30s
- Core: Anti‑rotation holds 4 × 10–15s/side

Week 10
- Slight increase loads where appropriate. Add tempo eccentrics for one main lift each lower day (3–4s lowering).
- Continue to progress single‑leg strength and isometrics.

Week 11
- Heavy week: attempt a 1–3RM for safe compounds like belt squat and hip thrust (not deep free squat). If client comfortable, test heavy single for confidence, but keep conservative and stop if knee reactive.
- Keep Nordic eccentrics and rotary control drills high quality.

Week 12 (taper / ski readiness)
- Reduce volume and slightly lower intensity; focus on explosiveness without impact: fast concentric lifts (e.g., lighter hip thrusts 3 × 3) and reactive control (rapid but low‑impact lateral steps).
- Final sessions emphasize movement quality, balance, and mobility. Do short ski‑specific metabolic session: 4–6 × 40s on skierg or lateral stepper at high but sustainable intensity, full recovery between intervals.
- Conclude with a return‑to‑ski checklist: pain‑free controlled single‑leg holds, ability to eccentrically control descent, no effusion or instability.

Sample session progressions & load notes
- Box squats/belt squats are the primary squat substitute. Box height should keep knee flexion ≤90°. If painfree, small increases in depth may be introduced only late in phase 3 and with caution.
- Use leg press (plate loaded) with range stops or an adjustable sled to train quads without deep flexion. Limit platform angle and foot position to reduce knee shear.
- For unilateral: prefer step‑ups and split squats with limited ROM; front foot elevated split squat only if knee comfortable.
- Eccentric work: Nordic hamstrings and 3–5s eccentrics on RDLs are excellent to build tendon resilience for skiing decelerations.

Conditioning and ski‑specific drills (integrate 1–2× week low impact)
- Skierg: interval work (20–40s efforts) for metabolic and upper body ski endurance.
- Lateral stepper or slideboard (no jumps): 30–60s intervals to mimic lateral loading and coordination.
- Agility with low impact: lateral cone steps, controlled change of direction at low speed.
- Neuromuscular training: single‑leg balance on foam or wobble board 2–3 × 60s.

Rehab/physio integration
- Maintain or add physiotherapy exercises that focus on:
  - Quad activation around 0–60° (isometrics and straight leg raises)
  - Hip abductor strengthening (band walks, clams, side‑lying hip abductions)
  - VMO neuromuscular control drills if prescribed
  - Knee ROM only to tolerated levels, guided by physio
- Ice and compression after any higher load sessions if swelling appears. Monitor range of motion and effusion daily.

Nutrition and recovery
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day (even distribution across meals).
- Calories: maintain or small surplus (+150–300 kcal/day) if aiming for muscle gain with strength; otherwise maintenance is acceptable.
- Carbohydrates around training to support performance (moderate: 3–5 g/kg/day depending on activity).
- Prioritize sleep 7–9 h nightly.
- Supplement considerations: vitamin D if deficient, creatine monohydrate 3–5 g/day for strength and recovery (unless contraindicated), omega‑3 for anti‑inflammatory benefits.
- Hydration and anti‑inflammatory strategies as needed; consult medical team before NSAIDs long‑term.

How to progress and regress
- Progress: increase load 2.5–5% when all prescribed reps completed with good form; for main lifts, add sets before adding load if technique needs more practice.
- Regress: reduce ROM, switch to belt squat or leg press, reduce load, increase assistance (bands) or increase reps with lower weight.
- If knee pain arises (≥4/10), stop the provoking exercise, reduce range/load, refer back to physio if persistent.

Return to skiing timeline recommendation
- This 12‑week program builds strength and robustness; before on‑snow return, perform functional assessment: single‑leg squat control, ability to sustain 30–60s lateral stepper intervals pain‑free, ability to perform eccentric decelerations without swelling. Consider an on‑snow gradual reintroduction: easy groomed runs for first day, limited duration, no off‑piste or big bumps until confidence and control returns.

Notes for your coaching
- Track pain, swelling, and functional markers weekly. Communicate with the client’s surgeon/physio for any concerning signs.
- Adjust individual exercise selection to client tolerance (e.g., swap Bulgarian split squat for step‑ups if knee bothers).
- Emphasize technique coaching on all lifts, especially hip hinge and knee tracking.

If you want, I can:
- Convert this to a printable 12‑week sheet with week‑by‑week load targets and progression percentage suggestions (e.g., exact kg progression).
- Provide a day‑by‑day warm‑up and mobility sequence tailored to the client’s current deficits.
- Suggest a sample nutrition plan with calorie targets for his bodyweight — if you share his weight and target body composition.
